lede: Some differences between people come in a few separate kinds; others come in every size in between. One question, counted or measured, decides the name of the variation and the graph you draw. Then there is where the differences come from: genes, the environment, or both.
can: Decide whether a characteristic shows continuous or discontinuous variation, and say why.
Choose and read the right graph, and turn a reading into a percentage of the class.
Explain the genetic and environmental causes of variation, including what a mutation is.

md: No two people in your class are exactly alike. Some differences come in a few fixed kinds: you can roll your tongue or you cannot. Others come in every size in between, like height.

md:
**Variation** is the differences between individuals in their **phenotype**, the characteristics each one actually has.

**Discontinuous variation** falls into a few **separate groups**, with nothing in between: **tongue rolling** and **hand dominance** are the examples.

**Continuous variation** can take **any value in a range**: **height** and **length** are the examples. You measure them, and every value in between is possible.

prompt: Hand span is measured in centimetres and can be any value in a range. Which type of variation does it show?
explain: Ask the one question: is it counted into groups, or measured on a scale? Hand span is measured with a ruler, and between any two spans there is always another, so it takes any value in a range. That is continuous variation. Tongue rolling, with its two separate groups, is the discontinuous kind.

md: Draw the graph the data already has in it. Blood groups are separate boxes: there is no blood group between A and B, so a **bar chart** leaves **gaps** between its bars. Height is a scale: between any two heights there is always another, so a **histogram** has its **bars touching**, each class running straight into the next.

title: Why the classes read 160 to 165, then 165 to 170
md: Each class runs from its lower value up to, but not including, its upper value. A height of exactly 165 cm goes in the 165 to 170 class, so every height has exactly one place and no gap is left.

prompt: A class records the body mass of every pupil. Which graph should display the results?
options: a histogram, with the bars touching
a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
answer: a histogram, with the bars touching
explain: Draw the graph the data already has in it. Body mass is measured on a scale, so any value in between is possible: the classes run straight into one another, and the bars touch. That is a histogram. Gaps between bars are for data that comes in separate groups.

md:
**Worked example.** What percentage of this class is shorter than 160 cm?
**Step 1: read the bars.** The 150 to 155 bar holds 1 and the 155 to 160 bar holds 4. So 1 + 4 = 5 pupils are shorter than 160 cm.

**Step 2: find the whole class.** Add every bar: 28 pupils.
**Step 3: divide, then multiply by 100.** 5 ÷ 28 × 100 = 17.9%, to 1 decimal place.
Check: this is part of the class, so it must be under 100%.

prompt: In a class of 25 pupils, 7 are left-handed. What percentage of the class is left-handed?
explain: A percentage is the group as a share of the whole class, out of 100: the group on top, the whole class underneath, then multiply by 100. Here the group is the 7 left-handed pupils and the class is 25, so 7 ÷ 25 × 100 = 28%. Check: a part of the class, so under 100%.

md:
Variation has a **genetic** basis and an **environmental** basis.

**Genetic.** A **mutation** is a **random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene**, so it can make something new. **Sexual reproduction** gives every child a new combination of its parents' genes. Both produce different phenotypes.

**Environmental.** Your surroundings shape how you develop: **diet** affects **height**, for example.

Most characteristics depend on both.

prompt: Which two things give variation a genetic basis?
explain: A genetic cause changes the genes an individual has. A mutation is a random change in a gene or in the number of chromosomes, and sexual reproduction deals every child a new combination of its parents' genes: both change the genes, so both are genetic. Diet and exercise act on the body, not the genes: they are the environment.

md: Cuttings taken from one plant all have the **same genes**. Give two of them different amounts of water and they grow to 40 cm and 30 cm, so the difference can only have come from the **environment**. Identical twins show the same thing in people.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Variation"
why: A short lesson on the causes of variation, made for another exam board: read the note beside it before you watch.

title: What this clip will not cover
md: Clips made for other boards cover the causes of variation, but those exams do not ask about **continuous** and **discontinuous** variation or which graph goes with each. CCEA does, so that part comes from this lesson. Types of mutation, if they appear, are not on this specification.

prompt: Two cuttings from the same plant grow to different heights. Because they have the same ______, the difference must be caused by the environment.
answer: genes | gene | genetic material | dna | alleles | genetic makeup | genetic make-up | genetic information | genotype | genetic code
explain: Cuttings are pieces of one plant, so every cutting carries exactly the same genes. A difference between two things with the same genes cannot come from the genes; only the environment is left, and here the environment that differed was the water. So the word is genes.

md:
Tell **continuous** variation (any value in a range) from **discontinuous** (separate groups), with an example of each.
Choose the graph and say why: a **histogram** with bars touching, or a **bar chart** with gaps.
Read a bar chart or histogram and turn a count into a **percentage** of the class.
Name the genetic causes, **mutation** and **sexual reproduction**, and define a mutation.
Explain an **environmental** cause, and why most characteristics depend on both.

Variation turns up as short parts inside a bigger B2 question, most often on the Foundation paper. The first mark is usually the type of variation or a reading from a graph; the second is the reason or the percentage. Stuck? Ask one question of the characteristic: was it counted into groups, or measured on a scale? Everything else follows from the answer.
